newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya's Moi warns opposition against choas.
newsitem.headline: Kenya's Moi warns opposition against choas.

text.p: Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi said on Friday he would take decisive action against any opposition attempt to bring choas to the country.
Moi's remarks were in response to a warning by opposition MPs that Kenya could slide into violence unless constitutional reforms were enacted before elections due this year.
Moi, aged 73 and in power for the last 19 years, swiftly challenged the opposition to take the debate on reforms to parliament where his ruling party holds a majority.
Moi spoke in the western town of Kisii few hours after the latest stand by the opposition.

"Those pressing for reforms must allow parliament to convene and address the matter. Two thirds parliamentary majority will have to approve the direction the amendment would have to take," Moi said in remarks relayed by his official press unit.
"The government will take decisive action to arrest any planned chaos," he added.
Moi on Thursday lambasted Western nations for urging dialogue with the opposition to end the east African nation's recent bout of unrest.
James Orengo, deputy leader of the opposition, warned Moi of a rebellion similar to that which ended Mobutu Sese Seko's rule in Zaire unless the president gave in to the clamour for reforms.

"Those who make peaceful change impossible make violent change inevitable. The consequences for rigidity on the part of the government will open up new options. And those who do not want to go the way the people go may become irrelevant," he said.

At a news conference in Nairobi, eleven opposition MPs also urged Kenya's business community to join in the campaign for reforms which this week escalated into the country's worst political unrest since pluralist politics returned in 1991.
The business community urged Moi to fix an early date for elections to decide Kenya's destiny and calm local financial markets.
Orengo gave no details on opposition plans to carry out their threats but said recent disturbances demonstrated the depth of popular resentment to Moi's government.

"We are saying no reforms, no elections. We are committed to an extent that we will ensure there are no elections. Kenyans have the capacity to make this country ungovernable. We are in the beginning of a revolution," Orongo said.

Nine people died in the unrest on Monday when the opposition called for rallies to press Moi into reforms before the elections. Further violence erupted on Wednesday when university students clashed with police and paramilitary forces.

The opposition, backed by churches, students and human rights groups, wants Moi to allow free access to the media, overhaul of the state appointed Electoral Commission and a repeal of a colonial act which regulates political assemblies.
But Moi, a reluctant convert to pluralism, only accepted multi-party elections in 1992 after heavy pressure from lifeblood western donors.
Vowing to resist the opposition's demands, Moi has employed strong arm tactics to assert his authority against protesters, resulting in this week's deaths.
This week's unrest prompted a total of 20 western countries led by the United States to press Moi to open a dialogue with opposition-backed groups.

The rising political temperature has hit markets hard with the shilling currency taking a beating and the Nairobi bourse plunging to a year low on Monday. But the governor of the Central Bank, Micah Cheserem, said the market was overreacting.
Cheserem said his bank offloaded up to $29 million to calm a jittery foreign exchange market. He said the intervention had helped recoup huge Kenyan shilling losses.

Kenya's usually divided opposition is looking forward to a boost when fiery Moslem preacher and activist, Sheikh Khalid Balala, returns on Saturday to Kenya after two years of forced exile in Germany.
